category.name: Azure
category.description: Incidents in Azure resources: storage, Key Vault, compute, AKS, App Service, monitoring and subscription-level control plane abuse.

playbooks.name: Storage account exposed by public container or leaked SAS token
playbooks.summary: Use when a blob container was found with anonymous access enabled, or an account-level SAS token or storage key appears in a repo, ticket, paste site, or client-side code.

preparation: Enable StorageRead, StorageWrite and StorageDelete diagnostic logs on every storage account to Log Analytics or Event Hub
Assign Azure Policy to deny allowBlobPublicAccess=true and audit allowSharedKeyAccess on storage accounts
Keep an inventory of which apps legitimately issue SAS tokens and their expected expiry and permissions
Confirm the IR role can run az storage account keys renew and rotate user delegation keys
identification: Parse the leaked SAS token for sv, ss, srt, sp, se and sip to learn scope, permissions and expiry
Determine whether the SAS is account-level, service-level, or user-delegation by its signing key (skoid present or not)
List containers with publicAccess set to blob or container using az storage container list --query
Search StorageBlobLogs for AuthenticationType SAS or Anonymous from IPs outside the known app ranges
Identify where the token was published and the earliest timestamp it was publicly reachable
containment: Set publicAccess to off on exposed containers and disable allowBlobPublicAccess on the account
Rotate the storage account key that signed the leaked SAS (key1 or key2) to invalidate every token it issued
Revoke user delegation keys with az storage account revoke-delegation-keys if the SAS was user-delegation
Restrict the account network rules to selected VNets and trusted IPs while apps are re-keyed
eradication: Remove the token or key from the repo history, paste, or ticket and request takedown where third-party hosted
Replace hard-coded SAS in client code with short-lived user-delegation SAS issued by a backend
Update every app connection string that used the rotated key, sourcing it from Key Vault references
recovery: Verify apps reconnect after key rotation by checking 403 rates in StorageBlobLogs
Re-enable public access only for containers with a documented business need and static public content
Compare blob inventory against a pre-incident inventory to confirm no blobs were overwritten or added
lessons: Add a detection for anonymous GetBlob or ListBlobs on accounts that are not tagged as public content
Record which data classifications were readable and feed the count into the privacy impact assessment
Evaluate disabling shared key authorization so only Entra-authorized access and user-delegation SAS remain
Add secret scanning for sig= and AccountKey= patterns in source control pre-commit and CI

splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=mscs:azure:eventhub category=StorageRead properties.accountName=<storage_account> (properties.authenticationType=SAS OR properties.authenticationType=Anonymous) | stats count sum(properties.responseBodySize) as bytes values(operationName) as ops by callerIpAddress, properties.authenticationType | sort - bytes

splunk.title: Storage key regeneration and public access changes

splunk.title: First and last use of the leaked SAS signature
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=mscs:azure:eventhub category=StorageRead properties.accountName=<storage_account> uri="*sig=*" | rex field=uri "se=(?<sas_expiry>[^&]+)" | stats min(_time) as first max(_time) as last dc(callerIpAddress) as ips by sas_expiry | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

playbooks.name: Mass blob download from a storage account
playbooks.summary: Use when egress or GetBlob volume from a storage account spikes far above baseline, suggesting bulk exfiltration with a valid key, SAS, or Entra identity.

preparation: Baseline daily Egress and Transactions metrics per storage account in Azure Monitor
Create a metric alert on Egress greater than three times the 14-day average for sensitive accounts
Tag storage accounts with data classification so responders can prioritize which spikes matter
Retain StorageBlobLogs for at least 90 days to reconstruct object-level access
identification: Chart the Egress metric for the account to bound the start and end of the spike
Group StorageBlobLogs GetBlob events by requesterObjectId, callerIpAddress and userAgentHeader
Check whether the user agent is AzCopy, Storage Explorer, rclone or a custom SDK client
Build the list of container and blob paths read during the window and their classification
Correlate the requesterObjectId with Entra sign-ins or service principal activity in the same window
containment: Remove the RBAC data-plane role (Storage Blob Data Reader or higher) from the identity performing the download
Rotate account keys if the access used SharedKey authentication
Add a firewall rule denying the destination caller IPs and switch default action to Deny
eradication: Disable or reset the credentials of the identity that performed the download
Remove any lifecycle, replication, or object replication policy that copies data to an unknown account
Delete any stored access policies on containers that were created during the incident window
recovery: Re-grant data-plane access only to identities that still need it, scoped to specific containers
Enable private endpoints for the account and remove public network access where feasible
Monitor Egress for two weeks after closure to confirm it returns to baseline
lessons: Measure time from egress spike to alert acknowledgement and tune the threshold
Assess whether Defender for Storage would have flagged the unusual data extraction
Document the exact blob list exposed and hand it to legal for notification analysis

splunk.title: Top downloaders by bytes from a storage account
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=mscs:azure:eventhub category=StorageRead operationName=GetBlob properties.accountName=<storage_account> | eval mb=round('properties.responseBodySize'/1048576,1) | stats sum(mb) as total_mb count as reads dc(uri) as blobs values(properties.userAgentHeader) as ua by callerIpAddress, identity.requester.objectId | sort - total_mb

splunk.title: Hourly GetBlob volume to bound the exfil window
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=mscs:azure:eventhub category=StorageRead operationName=GetBlob properties.accountName=<storage_account> | timechart span=1h count sum(properties.responseBodySize) as bytes

splunk.title: RBAC data-plane role assignments on the account
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity operationName.value="Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write" resourceId="*<storage_account>*" | table _time caller properties.requestbody status.value

playbooks.name: VM Run Command used to execute code on Azure VMs
playbooks.summary: Use when Activity Log shows runCommand actions or the Custom Script Extension deployed on VMs by an unexpected identity, indicating remote code execution through the control plane.

preparation: Send Activity Log for all subscriptions to the SIEM and alert on virtualMachines/runCommand/action
Restrict Virtual Machine Contributor and custom roles that include runCommand to a small admin group
Ensure Defender for Servers or EDR is onboarded so in-guest execution is recorded
identification: List runCommand/action and extensions/write operations by caller and target VM in Activity Log
Retrieve the script content from C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.CPlat.Core.RunCommandWindows on Windows guests
Check /var/lib/waagent/run-command/download on Linux guests for the executed script and output
Determine whether the caller is a user, service principal, or managed identity and where it signed in from
Review EDR process trees under the guest agent for child processes spawned by the script
containment: Remove the caller's role assignment that grants Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/runCommand/action
Isolate affected VMs with an NSG deny rule or Defender for Endpoint device isolation
Delete any managed run command resources (runCommands/write) left attached to the VM
eradication: Remove persistence created by the script such as new local users, scheduled tasks, or cron entries
Uninstall any Custom Script Extension added during the incident with az vm extension delete
Reset local admin credentials on affected VMs via the VMAccess extension from a trusted admin
recovery: Rebuild VMs from a known-good image if the script installed tooling you cannot fully enumerate
Re-enable network access only after EDR scans of the guest come back clean
Confirm no further runCommand events occur from the removed identity
lessons: Create a custom role baseline that excludes runCommand from general contributor roles
Add a detection for runCommand executed outside change windows or by non-admin identities
Review whether just-in-time privileged access would have blocked the caller

splunk.title: Run Command and extension deployments by caller
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity (operationName.value="Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/runCommand/action" OR operationName.value="Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/write" OR operationName.value="Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/runCommands/write") | stats count values(resourceId) as vms min(_time) as first by caller, callerIpAddress | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: Processes spawned by the Azure guest agent run command handler
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("RunCommandExtension.exe","CustomScriptHandler.exe","waagent") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

playbooks.name: Unauthorized VMs or scale sets deployed for cryptomining
playbooks.summary: Use when GPU or high-core VMs, scale sets, or quota increases appear in unusual regions, or Defender alerts on mining pool traffic, indicating a compromised identity is mining on your bill.

preparation: Apply an Azure Policy allowed-locations and allowed-VM-SKU list to every production subscription
Set budget alerts per subscription that notify security as well as finance
Keep a list of regions and GPU SKUs the business actually uses
identification: Query Activity Log for virtualMachines/write and virtualMachineScaleSets/write in unexpected regions
Check for Microsoft.Capacity quota increase requests submitted by the same caller
Inspect VM custom data or cloud-init for miner download commands and pool URLs
Look for outbound traffic to mining pool ports such as 3333, 4444, 5555 and 14444 in NSG flow logs
Identify the identity that created the resources and how it authenticated
containment: Stop and deallocate the mining VMs and scale sets to halt spend while preserving disks
Snapshot one OS disk for forensics before deleting the rest
Disable the creating identity and revoke its sessions or client secrets
eradication: Delete the attacker-created resource groups, VMs, NICs, public IPs and disks after evidence capture
Remove any new service principals, role assignments, or subscriptions the identity created
Revert quota increases that were requested by the attacker
recovery: File a billing support case with Microsoft documenting the fraudulent consumption
Confirm cost per day returns to baseline in Cost Management over the following week
Re-enable the legitimate identity with new credentials and narrowed scope if it was a real workload
lessons: Measure hours of mining before detection and the total cost incurred
Add a detection for first-time VM SKU families or regions per subscription
Decide whether GPU SKUs require an approval workflow before quota is granted

splunk.title: VM and scale set creation by region and caller
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity (operationName.value="Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write" OR operationName.value="Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachineScaleSets/write") status.value=Succeeded | rex field=resourceId "(?i)resourceGroups/(?<rg>[^/]+)" | stats count dc(resourceId) as resources values(rg) as rgs by caller, callerIpAddress | sort - resources

splunk.title: Outbound connections to common mining pool ports
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (3333,4444,5555,7777,14444) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | sort - count

splunk.title: Quota increase requests
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity operationName.value="Microsoft.Capacity/*" OR operationName.value="Microsoft.Quota/quotas/write" | table _time caller operationName.value resourceId status.value

playbooks.name: Key Vault secrets read in bulk by an unusual identity
playbooks.summary: Use when Key Vault AuditEvent logs show one identity listing and reading many secrets, keys, or certificates in a short window, especially from a new IP or a user rather than an app.

preparation: Enable AuditEvent diagnostic logs on every Key Vault and send them to the SIEM
Use Azure RBAC permission model on vaults so access changes appear in Activity Log
Record which applications read which secrets so per-identity baselines are possible
Document owners for each secret so rotation can be coordinated quickly
identification: Count SecretGet, SecretList, KeyGet and CertificateGet operations per identity per vault
Identify the full list of secret names read by the suspect identity
Check whether the vault access policy or RBAC assignment was changed shortly before the reads
Map each read secret to the system it unlocks (database, API, storage key, certificate private key)
Correlate the caller IP with sign-in logs to see if it is a stolen session or app credential
containment: Remove the identity's Key Vault Secrets User or access policy on the vault
Enable vault firewall to selected networks and private endpoint only
Prioritize rotating secrets that grant production data access or signing ability
eradication: Rotate every secret, key and certificate the identity read, starting with highest impact
Revoke and reissue certificates whose private keys were exportable and read
Reset the suspect identity's credentials and remove any federated credential it added
recovery: Confirm dependent apps pick up new secret versions and disable old versions
Watch the downstream systems for use of the old credentials as a sign of attacker reuse
Restore normal vault network rules only after the access review is complete
lessons: Add an alert on more than N distinct secrets read by one identity in an hour
Review whether humans need data-plane read access to production vaults at all
Track mean time to rotate all exposed secrets as a recovery metric

splunk.title: Distinct secrets read per identity
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=mscs:azure:eventhub category=AuditEvent resourceType=VAULTS (operationName=SecretGet OR operationName=SecretList OR operationName=KeyGet OR operationName=CertificateGet) | stats dc(id) as items count values(operationName) as ops by identity.claim.upn, identity.claim.appid, callerIpAddress, Resource | sort - items

splunk.title: Key Vault access policy and role changes
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity (operationName.value="Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/accessPolicies/write" OR operationName.value="Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write" OR (operationName.value="Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write" resourceId="*Microsoft.KeyVault*")) | table _time caller operationName.value resourceId

splunk.title: Use of rotated secrets after containment (401s from old creds)
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=mscs:azure:eventhub category=AuditEvent Resource=<vault_name> httpStatusCode=403 | stats count by callerIpAddress, identity.claim.appid, operationName

playbooks.name: Key Vault or its secrets deleted and purged
playbooks.summary: Use when a Key Vault, keys, or secrets are deleted and purged, or purge protection is being bypassed, which can destroy encryption keys and break dependent services permanently.

preparation: Enforce soft delete with 90-day retention and purge protection on all vaults via Azure Policy
Back up customer-managed keys used for disk, storage, and SQL encryption to a separate vault
Limit Key Vault Purge Operator and Key Vault Contributor roles to break-glass admins
identification: Find SecretDelete, KeyDelete, SecretPurge, KeyPurge and VaultDelete events and their caller
List soft-deleted vaults with az keyvault list-deleted and soft-deleted secrets with az keyvault secret list-deleted
Identify which disks, storage accounts, or SQL TDE protectors used the deleted keys
Check whether purge protection was enabled or whether the vault was created without it
containment: Remove delete and purge permissions from the caller identity immediately
Place a CanNotDelete resource lock on the vault and its resource group
Pause automation pipelines that might recreate or overwrite the vault with an empty one
eradication: Recover the soft-deleted vault with az keyvault recover before retention expires
Recover individual soft-deleted keys and secrets with az keyvault key recover and secret recover
Revoke the caller's sessions and rotate any credentials it could have used
recovery: Restore purged keys from backup blobs using az keyvault key restore into the recovered vault
Validate encrypted VMs, storage accounts and databases can unwrap their keys again
Enable purge protection on the recovered vault if it was missing
lessons: Inventory any data that is permanently unrecoverable due to purged keys and report it
Alert on any SecretPurge or KeyPurge operation regardless of caller
Review why the caller had purge rights and remove them from standing roles

splunk.title: Key Vault delete and purge operations
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=mscs:azure:eventhub category=AuditEvent (operationName=SecretDelete OR operationName=SecretPurge OR operationName=KeyDelete OR operationName=KeyPurge OR operationName=CertificatePurge) | stats count values(id) as items by Resource, identity.claim.upn, callerIpAddress, operationName

splunk.title: Vault-level delete and purge in Activity Log
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity (operationName.value="Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/delete" OR operationName.value="Microsoft.KeyVault/locations/deletedVaults/purge/action") | table _time caller callerIpAddress resourceId status.value

playbooks.name: Managed identity token stolen from IMDS and used elsewhere
playbooks.summary: Use when a managed identity's access token appears in use from outside its host resource, or a compromised VM, container or app may have queried IMDS to steal identity tokens.

preparation: Enable Entra service principal sign-in logs (ManagedIdentitySignInLogs) export to the SIEM
Scope each managed identity to the minimum resources it needs instead of subscription-wide roles
Record which resources host each user-assigned managed identity
identification: Pull ManagedIdentitySignInLogs for the identity and note resource requested and source resource
Compare callerIpAddress on Activity Log actions by the identity against the host resource's egress IPs
On the host, look for processes calling 169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token unexpectedly
Check App Service and Functions for requests to IDENTITY_ENDPOINT with the X-IDENTITY-HEADER value
List every action the identity performed during the window across subscriptions
containment: Remove role assignments from the managed identity to cut access while tokens are still valid
Isolate the host resource that leaked the token for forensic review
Block the external IPs seen using the token with Conditional Access for workload identities where licensed
eradication: Fix the SSRF or code execution flaw on the host that allowed IMDS access
Replace the user-assigned identity with a new one if the old one is suspected of long-term abuse
Remove any resources or role assignments the stolen token created
recovery: Reassign minimal roles to the new identity and redeploy the workload
Confirm no further activity from the old identity's object ID after tokens expire
Add egress filtering to block IMDS from application containers that do not need it
lessons: Detect managed identity Activity Log calls whose IP is not an Azure IP of the host
Review application code for SSRF paths that can reach link-local addresses
Document how long a stolen managed identity token stays valid in your tenant (default 24h)

splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity caller=<mi_object_id> | stats count values(operationName.value) as ops min(_time) as first by callerIpAddress | convert ctime(first) | sort - count

splunk.title: Host processes reaching IMDS token endpoint
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*169.254.169.254/metadata/identity*" by Web.src Web.http_user_agent Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

playbooks.name: Automation account runbook or webhook added as a backdoor
playbooks.summary: Use when a new or modified Azure Automation runbook, schedule, or webhook appears, especially one running as a privileged Run As or managed identity, giving the attacker persistent execution.

preparation: Enable JobLogs, JobStreams and AuditEvent diagnostics on every Automation account
Keep runbooks in source control with sync so unexpected edits are visible
Review which identity each Automation account runs as and its role scope
identification: List runbooks/write, runbooks/draft/write, webhooks/write and schedules/write in Activity Log
Export the runbook content with az automation runbook show-content and review it for credential theft or new accounts
Check webhook URIs and creation dates since a webhook lets anyone with the URL trigger the runbook
Review JobStreams for output from jobs that ran the suspect runbook
Identify hybrid runbook workers the runbook can execute on
containment: Unpublish or delete the suspect runbook and disable linked schedules
Delete webhooks created during the incident window
Remove privileged roles from the Automation account's managed identity temporarily
eradication: Revert remaining runbooks to the versions in source control
Remove any credentials, certificates, or variables added to the Automation account by the attacker
Hunt for resources or identities created by the backdoor runbook jobs
recovery: Restore legitimate schedules and reassign least-privilege roles to the account identity
Confirm hybrid workers show no residual jobs from the backdoor
Monitor JobLogs for unexpected runbook names over the next month
lessons: Alert on any runbook publish outside the source control sync identity
Assess retiring Run As accounts in favor of scoped managed identities
Add Automation accounts to the privileged resource review cycle

splunk.title: Runbook, webhook and schedule changes
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity operationName.value IN ("Microsoft.Automation/automationAccounts/runbooks/write","Microsoft.Automation/automationAccounts/runbooks/publish/action","Microsoft.Automation/automationAccounts/webhooks/write","Microsoft.Automation/automationAccounts/schedules/write") | table _time caller callerIpAddress operationName.value resourceId

splunk.title: Automation jobs by runbook name
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=mscs:azure:eventhub category=JobLogs | stats count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last values(ResultType) as results by RunbookName_s, Caller_s | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

playbooks.name: Activity Log or resource diagnostic settings deleted
playbooks.summary: Use when diagnostic settings that export Activity Log or resource logs are deleted or redirected, a common defense evasion step that blinds the SOC before further actions.

preparation: Deploy diagnostic settings via Azure Policy DeployIfNotExists so deletions are remediated
Alert in the SIEM when a subscription's Activity Log stops arriving for more than 30 minutes
Keep a secondary log path such as a management group level diagnostic setting
identification: Find Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/delete and write operations and their caller
Check whether a setting was modified to send logs to a workspace or storage account outside your tenant
Determine the gap window per subscription by finding the last event received before deletion
Review all other actions the caller performed during and after the gap
containment: Recreate the deleted diagnostic settings pointing to the approved workspace and Event Hub
Remove Monitoring Contributor or Owner rights from the caller
Apply a deny assignment or policy blocking diagnosticSettings/delete for non-platform identities
eradication: Delete any attacker-controlled destination added to diagnostic settings
Run a Resource Graph query to confirm every subscription and key resource has the approved settings
Disable the credentials of the identity that removed logging
recovery: Pull the 90-day Activity Log from the portal or REST API to fill the gap in the SIEM
Verify new events from each subscription are arriving in Splunk again
Trigger a Policy remediation task for any non-compliant resources
lessons: Track the duration of the logging gap and what could not be reconstructed
Add a heartbeat search per subscription for Activity Log ingestion
Restrict who can modify diagnostic settings to the platform pipeline identity

splunk.title: Diagnostic settings deleted or changed
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity (operationName.value="Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/delete" OR operationName.value="Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/write") | table _time caller callerIpAddress resourceId operationName.value properties.requestbody

splunk.title: Subscriptions that went quiet (ingestion gap)
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false latest(_time) as last_seen where index=azure sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity by subscriptionId | eval minutes_silent=round((now()-last_seen)/60) | where minutes_silent>30 | convert ctime(last_seen)

playbooks.name: Defender for Cloud plans disabled or alerts suppressed
playbooks.summary: Use when Defender for Cloud pricing tiers are set to Free, auto-provisioning is disabled, or suppression rules are added that hide alerts, suggesting an attacker is disabling detection.

preparation: Enforce required Defender plans with Azure Policy at the management group level
Restrict Security Admin role to the security team and monitor its assignment
Export Defender alerts continuously to the SIEM so suppression is visible
identification: Search Activity Log for Microsoft.Security/pricings/write setting pricingTier to Free
Look for Microsoft.Security/alertsSuppressionRules/write and review the rule criteria
Check for autoProvisioningSettings or Defender for Endpoint integration being turned off
Review Defender alerts generated just before the plan change for the activity being hidden
containment: Re-enable the disabled Defender plans on each affected subscription
Delete suppression rules not created by the security team
Remove Security Admin or Owner from the identity that made the changes
eradication: Re-run Defender recommendations and investigate any alerts on resources during the blind window
Reinstall Defender for Endpoint on servers where the extension was removed
Reset credentials and sessions for the caller identity
recovery: Confirm Defender plans show Standard tier for all required resource types
Verify alert flow into the SIEM with a Defender sample alert
Review Secure Score for regressions introduced during the incident
lessons: Add a high-priority detection on any pricings/write that lowers a tier
Require approval for new suppression rules via change management
Measure the time Defender coverage was off and what it would have caught

splunk.title: Defender plan downgrades and suppression rules
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity (operationName.value="Microsoft.Security/pricings/write" OR operationName.value="Microsoft.Security/alertsSuppressionRules/write" OR operationName.value="Microsoft.Security/autoProvisioningSettings/write") | table _time caller subscriptionId operationName.value properties.requestbody

splunk.title: Defender alerts preceding the change
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=mscs:azure:security:alert earliest=-7d | stats count values(AlertDisplayName) as alerts by CompromisedEntity, Severity | sort - count

playbooks.name: Network security group rule opened management ports to the internet
playbooks.summary: Use when an NSG or Azure Firewall rule is created or changed to allow RDP, SSH, WinRM or database ports from Any or 0.0.0.0/0, exposing workloads to scanning and brute force.

preparation: Assign Azure Policy to deny inbound NSG rules from Internet on ports 22, 3389, 5985 and 1433
Enable NSG or VNet flow logs and Traffic Analytics for production VNets
Offer Azure Bastion and just-in-time VM access so admins do not need open ports
identification: Find networkSecurityGroups/securityRules/write events and extract sourceAddressPrefix and destinationPortRange
List VMs and NICs attached to the modified NSG and their public IPs
Query flow logs for inbound connections allowed by the new rule since it was created
Check Windows Security 4625 and 4624 logon type 10, or sshd auth logs, on exposed hosts
Determine whether the change was made by a pipeline, an admin, or an unknown identity
containment: Delete the permissive rule or narrow its source to the admin IP range
Enable JIT access on affected VMs so ports open only on request
Block source IPs that successfully authenticated during the exposure window
eradication: Review exposed hosts for new accounts, services, or malware if any external logon succeeded
Reset local administrator passwords on hosts that received brute-force attempts
Revert any other network changes made by the same caller
recovery: Confirm flow logs show no further inbound traffic from the internet on management ports
Re-scan public IPs with your external attack surface tool to confirm closure
Document the approved remote access path for the team that opened the port
lessons: Measure exposure time and count of distinct scanning IPs observed
Move NSG rules into infrastructure as code with PR review
Add a detection on any NSG rule with source Internet or * and a management port

splunk.title: NSG rules allowing inbound from any source
splunk.spl: index=azure sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity operationName.value="Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/securityRules/write" status.value=Succeeded | spath input=properties.requestbody path=properties.sourceAddressPrefix output=src_prefix | spath input=properties.requestbody path=properties.destinationPortRange output=dport | search src_prefix IN ("*","0.0.0.0/0","Internet","Any") | table _time caller resourceId src_prefix dport

splunk.title: Inbound allowed flows on management ports
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count dc(All_Traffic.src) as sources from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.action=allowed All_Traffic.dest_port IN (22,3389,5985,5986,1433) All_Traffic.dest=<host_ip> by All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

splunk.title: Remote logons on exposed Windows hosts
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security (EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=10) OR EventCode=4625 host=<host> | stats count by EventCode, Source_Network_Address, Account_Name | sort - count

playbooks.name: Subscription transferred out of the tenant or Owner granted externally
playbooks.summary: Use when an Azure subscription is moved to another directory, billing ownership changes, or Owner is assigned to an external or guest account, risking loss of control over all its resources.

preparation: Set the tenant subscription policy to block subscriptions leaving or entering the directory
Restrict billing account owner and Global Administrator roles and monitor their use
Keep a current list of subscription IDs, their billing owners and management group placement
identification: Check Activity Log for Microsoft.Subscription/changeTenantRequest or rename and alias operations
Search for roleAssignments/write at subscription scope granting Owner to a guest or external object ID
Review billing account audit logs for transfer requests or accepted billing ownership changes
Confirm whether the subscription still appears under your tenant's management groups
Identify who initiated elevated access via Microsoft.Authorization/elevateAccess/action
containment: Remove Owner and User Access Administrator assignments that were not approved
Decline or cancel pending billing transfer requests in the billing portal
Disable the Global Administrator or billing admin account that initiated the change
eradication: Open a Microsoft support severity A case to reverse a completed directory transfer
Remove elevated access at root scope for any Global Admin who toggled it
Review the subscription for new resources, identities and keys created after the transfer
recovery: Move the subscription back under the correct management group and reapply policies
Re-establish RBAC from your documented baseline and re-enable diagnostics
Verify billing ownership and payment method are correct
lessons: Add a critical alert for elevateAccess/action and subscription directory changes
Evaluate privileged identity management for billing and tenant root roles
Document the time it took to regain control and the support escalation path

splunk.title: Subscription-scope Owner grants and elevate access

playbooks.name: Resource locks removed followed by mass resource deletion
playbooks.summary: Use when CanNotDelete or ReadOnly locks are removed and resource groups, VMs, databases, or storage are deleted in bulk, indicating destructive activity by an attacker or rogue insider.

preparation: Apply CanNotDelete locks to production resource groups and restrict locks/delete to a small role
Keep backups and soft delete for VMs, SQL, storage and Key Vault in separate subscriptions
Export resource inventory daily via Azure Resource Graph for rebuild reference
identification: Find Microsoft.Authorization/locks/delete events and the identity that removed them
Count resourceGroups/delete and other delete operations by caller over the incident window
Build the list of deleted resources from Activity Log and compare to yesterday's inventory
Check whether delete operations are still in progress (status Accepted or Started)
containment: Disable the deleting identity and revoke its refresh tokens and secrets
Re-add CanNotDelete locks on remaining production resource groups
Assign a deny policy or deny assignment blocking delete actions at management group scope temporarily
eradication: Remove any role assignments the identity added for itself or others before the deletion
Check automation accounts, pipelines and Logic Apps for scheduled destructive jobs
Rotate credentials for the service connection used if deletes came from a pipeline
recovery: Restore VMs and disks from Recovery Services vault in priority order
Recover deleted SQL databases from point-in-time restore and storage from soft delete
Redeploy networking and app infrastructure from infrastructure as code templates
Validate business services end to end before reopening traffic
lessons: Alert on any locks/delete followed by more than five deletes from the same caller in an hour
Measure recovery time per tier and compare to RTO targets
Review separation between backup administrators and production owners

playbooks.name: AKS cluster compromised via exposed API or stolen kubeconfig
playbooks.summary: Use when an AKS cluster shows unknown kubectl activity, privileged pods, listClusterAdminCredential calls, or containers running unexpected images in kube-system or default namespaces.

preparation: Enable kube-audit-admin and guard diagnostic categories on AKS clusters to the SIEM
Use Entra integration with local accounts disabled so listClusterAdminCredential is not usable
Restrict API server access with authorized IP ranges or private cluster
identification: Search Activity Log for managedClusters/listClusterAdminCredential/action and listClusterUserCredential

List pods with privileged, hostPID, hostNetwork or hostPath mounts across namespaces
Check images running in the cluster against your approved ACR registry list
Look for new ClusterRoleBindings granting cluster-admin
containment: Rotate cluster certificates with az aks rotate-certs to invalidate stolen admin kubeconfigs
Cordon nodes that ran attacker pods and apply a deny-all NetworkPolicy to affected namespaces
Restrict authorized IP ranges on the API server to the admin network
eradication: Delete attacker pods, DaemonSets, CronJobs and ClusterRoleBindings
Reimage or replace node pools that ran privileged attacker containers
Rotate secrets mounted into compromised namespaces and the kubelet managed identity's access
recovery: Redeploy workloads from GitOps or pipeline to a clean node pool
Enable Azure Policy for AKS to block privileged pods and unapproved registries
Confirm audit logs show only expected identities over the following week
lessons: Disable local accounts on every AKS cluster and track exceptions
Add detections for exec into pods in production namespaces
Review how the kubeconfig or token left a trusted device

playbooks.name: Function App code or settings modified to add a backdoor
playbooks.summary: Use when an Azure Function's code, deployment package, app settings, or function keys change unexpectedly, possibly turning it into an HTTP-triggered backdoor using its managed identity.

preparation: Deploy Function Apps only from pipelines with run-from-package and disable portal editing
Send FunctionAppLogs and App Service audit logs to the SIEM
Track function keys and host keys as secrets with owners
identification: Find sites/config/write, sites/functions/write, and publishxml or zipdeploy events in Activity Log
Download the current package from WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE or Kudu and diff it against the release artifact
List function keys and host keys and check for keys created during the window
Review app settings for changed WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE URLs pointing to external storage
Query FunctionAppLogs and Application Insights requests for invocations from unusual IPs
containment: Stop the Function App or disable the suspicious function
Regenerate host and function keys and the master key
Remove role assignments from the app's managed identity until code is verified
eradication: Redeploy the last known-good release from the pipeline
Remove deployment credentials (publishing profile, FTP) and disable basic auth publishing
Delete any extra deployment slots added by the attacker
recovery: Restore managed identity roles to the documented minimum
Confirm the running package hash matches the pipeline artifact
Watch invocation logs for calls to the removed function route
lessons: Alert on zipdeploy or publish events not originating from the pipeline identity
Disable SCM basic auth across all App Service plans by policy
Review what the managed identity could reach and reduce it

playbooks.name: Web shell dropped on an Azure App Service
playbooks.summary: Use when an App Service shows new script files in wwwroot, Kudu console use, or HTTP requests to unexpected .aspx, .php, or .jsp paths that return 200, suggesting a web shell.

preparation: Enable AppServiceHTTPLogs, AppServiceFileAuditLogs and AppServiceConsoleLogs diagnostics
Put internet-facing App Services behind Front Door or Application Gateway WAF
Restrict SCM (Kudu) site access with access restrictions to admin networks

Download the site content via Kudu and diff it against the release artifact
Identify the initial entry point such as a vulnerable upload handler or framework CVE

Stop the app or swap traffic to a clean staging slot
Reset publishing credentials and disable FTP and SCM basic auth

Patch the vulnerable component that allowed the upload
Rotate connection strings and app settings secrets the shell could read from environment variables

Confirm HTTP logs show no further requests reaching the shell path
Review outbound connections from the app to detect lateral movement through VNet integration

Track the time between shell creation and first detection
Evaluate WAF rule sets for the exploit used

playbooks.name: Azure SQL server firewall opened to all IPs or Azure services
playbooks.summary: Use when an Azure SQL or SQL Managed Instance firewall rule allows 0.0.0.0–255.255.255.255, public network access is enabled, or Allow Azure services is toggled, exposing databases.

preparation: Enforce private endpoints and deny public network access on SQL servers via Azure Policy
Enable SQL auditing to Log Analytics or Event Hub and Defender for SQL
Require Entra-only authentication on SQL servers where possible

Set publicNetworkAccess to Disabled if private endpoints are available

eradication: Remove database users, logins or contained users created from external sessions
Check for new server-level firewall rules or virtual network rules added by the attacker
Review for exported BACPACs to unknown storage accounts
recovery: Confirm application connectivity through private endpoint or approved IPs
Verify audit logs show no external logins after closure
Run a vulnerability assessment on the database

Move SQL network configuration into reviewed infrastructure as code

playbooks.name: Logic App workflow created to exfiltrate data
playbooks.summary: Use when a Logic App is created or modified with connectors that read mailboxes, SharePoint, SQL, or storage and post data to an external HTTP endpoint or personal account.

preparation: Enable WorkflowRuntime diagnostic logs for Logic Apps to the SIEM
Restrict who can create API connections (Microsoft.Web/connections) to approved teams
Maintain an allow list of outbound HTTP endpoints used by integrations

Delete or revoke the API connections it uses so stored OAuth tokens stop working

Check for sibling workflows in other resource groups created by the same caller

Confirm no runs occur after disablement

playbooks.name: Azure DevOps personal access token leaked and used

playbooks.name: Azure Arc-connected server abused for remote execution
playbooks.summary: Use when Arc-enabled on-prem or multicloud servers receive unexpected extensions, run commands, or machine identity token use, giving a cloud identity a path into your datacenter.

playbooks.name: Backup vault soft delete disabled or backups deleted
playbooks.summary: Use when soft delete or immutability is turned off on a Recovery Services or Backup vault, backup items are stopped with data deletion, or policies are shortened, often a pre-ransomware step.
